newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian opposition looks to youth for votes.
newsitem.headline: Croatian opposition looks to youth for votes.

text.p: Croatia's opposition Social Liberal party hopes young people and city-dwellers will vote it into power across the country, putting the concerns of everyday life first in Sunday's municipal elections.

Zlatko Kramaric, mayor of Osijek and one of only seven opposition urban government leaders in Croatia, is confident he will be re-elected and says he hopes liberals will be voted into most town halls and more than half the counties.
This would give them strength in numbers, enabling them to form a lobby in government to push through legislation and hopefully take over the administration of larger cities.

President Franjo Tudjman's conservative nationalist HDZ party currently governs 17 of 21 counties. His y faces a centre-left opposition challenge in major cities in the regional elections on Sunday, which will include former rebel Serbs for the first time.
"It is as important to win in as many big towns as possible and to create a lobby to pressure the government," said Kramaric, a member of the Social Liberal Party (HSLS).
At a Friday evening rally in Osijek's baroque main square, hundreds of young people turned out to hear the youthful Kramaric, spontaneously cheering and applauding his speech.
In Zagreb's main square at the same time, Tudjman held his last election rally in front of one of the smaller crowds he has addressed, winning only mild applause.
"I'm sure the opposition is going to win (locally) all over Croatia, but I'm also sure Tudjman will win the presidential elections (this summer)," said Stevo Maglajic, 50, an engineer.
"It's not a problem as long as the opposition has power because he won't be able to govern his satellites as well as he has up until now."
"It's true that we have to look forward ... We want to see life become normal," said Nevenka Bjelotonic.
What concerned those at the rally were mundane realities of life such as schooling and infrastructure rather than thoughts of nationhood or defence, Tudjman's favourite themes.
Kramaric, 41, said his mayoral prerogatives had been constantly blocked at the county level, administered by HDZ nationalist Branimir Glavas, the region's main power broker.

"It's a shameful blockade because a big town like Osijek has no administrative power...You can have a project and the money but if they don't give you permission or keep stalling, it makes you look powerless and inadequate.
"One of the main problems has been how to explain to people that these are not presidential elections," Kramaric said, referring to party lists of Tudjman's HDZ headed with his name.

"The HDZ plays the card of emotions and statehood which is very precious for older Croatians. They cunningly equated their party with the state...But sooner or later people will all turn to their close interests and their everyday life."
Situated on the East Slavonian plain, Osijek is Croatia's fourth largest city and has the highest unemployment rate in the country with some 15,000 people out of work, Kramaric said.
Enclosed on three sides by the Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia, Osijek sits next to the old front line from Croatia's 1991 war for independence from federal Yugoslavia.
The town has lost around 70 percent of its industry and has been cut off from its economically vital hinterland since it fell into the hands of separatist Serbs six years ago.
Osijek lies on the Drava River and close to the Danube and has been an important trading centre and port since the 14th century.

Delegations from Switzerland, Italy, Slovenia and Hungary have visited Osijek but foreign investors are reluctant to hand over money until Eastern Slavonia is peacefully reintegrated in Croatia, due to happen after a U.N. administrative mandate in the region expires on July 15.
